newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Horn seen unchallenged as worried Socialists gather.
newsitem.headline: Horn seen unchallenged as worried Socialists gather.

text.p: Hungary's governing Socialist Party (MSZP) begins a two-day conference on Friday in sombre mood with the popularity of the party and its leader, Prime Minister Gyula Horn, plumbing new lows.

Less than a year ahead of elections and following two years of austerity which have seen real wages fall by over 15 percent, the MSZP trails both the opposition Smallholders and the Young Democrats while Horn figured 25th on a list of politicians cited in recent polls.

However, murmurs of discontent about Horn's leadership are to be kept well below the surface at the gathering, which formally is the continuation of a November 1995 congress specifically excluding the discussion of personnel issues.

"The most we can expect is some kind of suggestion that we need a new leadership if we are going to win the election but that position does not have too much support," Istvan Stumpf, head of politics at the Academy of Sciences, told Reuters.
The opposition to Horn centres on the intellectual liberal wing of the party headed by Ivan Vitanyi and former finance minister Laszlo Bekesi.
Bekesi attacked Horn this week for "unthought-out public statements" which undermined the government's credibility, and said new leadership was the only way to restore public confidence.
Political analyst Tibor Vidos believes the conference will at most call for a leadership vote in the autumn but this is unlikely to signal Horn's downfall.
"There is no challenger who can unite the party behind him." he said. "There will be no coup against Horn."
Popular foreign minister Laszlo Kovacs and former employment minister Magda Kosa are seen as the strongest candidates in any leadership vote but both have already sworn loyalty to Horn.
"The key members of the party leadership realise that, if they change leaders, it could cause some instability in the government," said Stumpf.

Even the party's current coalition with the even more unpopular Free Democrats is unlikely to be challenged, although Horn has made it clear that the Socialists will be open to other partners after the general election in spring 1998.
As a result, the congress is unlikely to cause Horn any headaches.

"Like all Socialist Party congresses over the last four years, internal fighting becomes vocal in the days ahead of the gathering, after which the congress itself puts on a show of unity," said Vidos.
"This will last for a few months before the disagreements start again"
